docs.title: oscompat
docs.text:
Cross-platform operating-system compatibility utilities for Go. It holds the code that differs between Windows and Unix-like systems (Linux, macOS), so that other modules do not carry platform-specific files of their own.

go get github.com/grokify/oscompat

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Solves Guide fs Permissions, paths, executables, file locks, durable renames fs process Signals, process groups, liveness, start time, exec process paths Config, data, cache and runtime directories paths id Unique identifiers that do not collide on Windows id tsync Timestamp comparison across filesystems tsync localnet Local inter-process sockets localnet testutil Test helpers that behave the same everywhere testutil

New here? Read Getting started. Writing tests that fail only on Windows? Read Writing tests that pass on Windows.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
oscompat has no dependencies. It imports the Go standard library and itself, and nothing else: no module outside the standard library, and not even golang.org/x/sys. A test in the module enforces it. That is what makes it safe for any module to import, including modules that keep their own dependency set small on purpose, such as ones that handle key material.

In return, modules are encouraged to import oscompat instead of keeping _windows.go and _unix.go files, build tags or runtime.GOOS checks of their own. Code that differs by operating system belongs here once, tested on every platform, so that callers read as portable code.

If a module needs a difference oscompat does not cover, add it here rather than beside the caller, using only the standard library.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text: All packages are tested on Linux, macOS and Windows.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: See the release notes and the changelog.

docs.title: fs: files, permissions, locks
docs.text:
fs holds what differs between Windows and Unix when working with files.

import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/fs"

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Mode bits are not enforced on Windows. Code that refuses a world-readable key file, and tests that assert 0600, are wrong there unless they ask first.

Function Behavior PermissionsEnforced() Whether the platform enforces mode bits; false on Windows IsPrivate(info) Owner-only. Always true where modes are not enforced CheckPrivate(info) An error matching ErrNotPrivate that names the mode; nil where modes are not enforced ChmodPrivate(f) Restricts an open file to its owner (0600); a failure is ignored where modes are not enforced WriteFilePrivate, MkdirAllPrivate Create a file or directory for the owner only PrivateFilePerm, PrivateDirPerm, DefaultFilePerm, DefaultDirPerm The usual modes as constants

Refusing a file other users can read:

info, err := os.Stat(path)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := fs.CheckPrivate(info); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", path, err)
}

In a test, assert only where modes mean something:

if fs.PermissionsEnforced() {
    info, _ := os.Stat(path)
    if err := fs.CheckPrivate(info); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
}

docs.title: File locks
docs.text:
unlock, err := fs.Lock(ctx, "/var/lib/myapp/state.lock")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer unlock()

Lock takes an exclusive advisory lock on a file, creating it (owner-only) if needed. It uses flock on Unix and LockFileEx on Windows.

  • It waits until the lock is free or ctx ends, and then returns the context's error. Give it a deadline.
  • The lock is held on an open handle, so the operating system releases it if the process dies, however it dies. A crashed holder never wedges everyone else.
  • Two calls in the same process exclude each other, as two processes do.
  • It is advisory: it excludes only callers that also take it.
  • unlock may be called more than once.
  • On a platform with no locking it returns ErrLockUnsupported. A caller that needs mutual exclusion should fail closed and not proceed without it.

Keep the lock file separate from the file it protects. Replacing the protected file by rename would otherwise swap the file the lock is held on.

docs.title: Durable renames
docs.text:
if err := fs.SyncDir(dir); err != nil {
    return err
}

A rename is durable across a crash only once the directory is flushed. SyncDir does that on Unix. On Windows, and wherever the platform has no way to ask, it does nothing and returns nil: a rename there is atomic and nothing stronger is available. You get the strongest guarantee the platform offers without a platform check.

The complete write-temp, flush, rename, flush-directory sequence is shown in Getting started.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Function Behavior ValidatePath(p) Rejects .. traversal with either separator SafeJoin(base, rel) Joins and refuses a result that escapes base NormalizePath(p) Converts to forward slashes, for storage OSPath(p) Converts to the platform's separator PathEqual, PathHasPrefix Compare with the platform's case rules IsExecutable(path) Mode bits on Unix; extension on Windows

Import the package you need. There is nothing to configure and nothing else to install, because the module has no dependencies.

docs.title: Which package for which problem
docs.text: You need to Use Keep two processes from writing a file at once fs.Lock Make a rename durable fs.SyncDir Refuse a file other users can read, or write one only the owner can fs.CheckPrivate, fs.WriteFilePrivate, fs.ChmodPrivate Know whether mode bits mean anything here fs.PermissionsEnforced Check a path from outside for .. fs.ValidatePath, fs.SafeJoin Find a config, data, cache or runtime directory paths.AppConfig, paths.AppData, paths.AppCache, paths.AppRuntime Stop a child process, or run one detached process.Signal, process.SetDetached Tell whether a recorded PID is still the same process process.Exists, process.StartTime Hand the terminal to another program process.Exec Generate an identifier id.Generate16, id.Generate32 Compare file modification times tsync.Equal, tsync.After Talk between local processes localnet.Listen, localnet.Dial Write tests that pass on Windows the guide, and testutil

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
Replace a file so that a crash leaves the old one or the new one, and so that two processes do not do it at once:

import (
    "context"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"

    "github.com/grokify/oscompat/fs"
)

func replace(ctx context.Context, path string, data []byte) error {
    unlock, err := fs.Lock(ctx, path+".lock")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer unlock()

    dir := filepath.Dir(path)
    tmp, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, filepath.Base(path)+".tmp-*")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer os.Remove(tmp.Name()) // a no-op once renamed

    if err := fs.ChmodPrivate(tmp); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if _, err := tmp.Write(data); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := tmp.Sync(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := tmp.Close(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := os.Rename(tmp.Name(), path); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return fs.SyncDir(dir)
}

None of it checks the operating system.

docs.title: Contributing a difference
docs.text: If you find yourself writing runtime.GOOS or a build tag, add it here instead, with a test, using only the standard library. See the policy.

docs.title: id: identifiers
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/id"

Identifiers built from the clock collide on Windows, where time.Now() advances in steps of about 15.6 ms and several values taken in a row are equal. id draws from crypto/rand instead.

spanID := id.Generate16()  // 16 hex characters (8 random bytes)
traceID := id.Generate32() // 32 hex characters (16 random bytes)
custom := id.Generate(4)   // 8 hex characters (N bytes is 2N characters)

Generate panics if crypto/rand fails, which does not happen on a working system.

These are random, not ordered. If you need identifiers that sort by creation time, use a time-ordered scheme such as UUIDv7 and keep the ordering in the identifier, not in a timestamp column.

docs.title: localnet: local sockets
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/localnet"

Unix uses domain sockets; Windows has them only in limited form. localnet gives both the same calls.

// Server
l, err := localnet.Listen("myapp")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer l.Close() // also removes the socket or port file

for {
    conn, err := l.Accept()
    // ...
}

// Client
conn, err := localnet.Dial("myapp")
Platform Mechanism Unix A domain socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or /tmp Windows A TCP listener on localhost on an ephemeral port, with the port recorded in a file for clients
  • Cleanup(name) removes a stale socket or port file left by a crash. It is safe to call when none exists.
  • SocketPath(name) reports the path or address, for logs.
  • An empty name is ErrInvalidName; a socket that already exists is ErrSocketExists.
  • Pick a name that is yours. Two applications that choose the same one will collide.

docs.title: paths: where files go
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/paths"

Each application directory follows the platform's convention and is created if it does not exist.

Function Linux macOS Windows AppConfig(name) ~/.config/<name> ~/Library/Application Support/<name> %APPDATA%\<name> AppData(name) ~/.local/share/<name> ~/Library/Application Support/<name> %LOCALAPPDATA%\<name> AppCache(name) ~/.cache/<name> ~/Library/Caches/<name> %LOCALAPPDATA%\cache\<name> AppRuntime(name) $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/<name> or /tmp/runtime-<uid>/<name> ~/Library/Application Support/<name> %LOCALAPPDATA%\run\<name> SystemAppConfig(name) /etc/<name> /etc/<name> %ProgramData%\<name> 
cfg, err := paths.AppConfig("myapp")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
  • The runtime directory is created 0700; the others 0755. On macOS and Windows it sits beside the application's other files rather than in a temporary location, so remove stale files from it at start-up.
  • Use the runtime directory for sockets and PID files, which should not survive a reboot.
  • Home() returns the user's home directory or ErrHomeNotFound.
  • An empty name is ErrInvalidAppName.
  • UserConfig, UserData, UserCache, UserRuntime and SystemConfig return the base directories without an application name or creating anything.

In tests, set the home directory with testutil.SetTempHomeDir.

docs.title: Writing Tests That Pass on Windows
docs.text: Most Windows-only test failures in Go projects come from a handful of platform differences. They are cheap to avoid when writing the code and tedious to diagnose from a CI log afterward. This guide lists them with the portable alternative for each.

docs.title: Wall-clock ties
docs.text:
The difference: time.Now() on Linux and macOS has nanosecond resolution. On Windows the clock advances in steps of roughly 0.5 to 15.6 ms, so values taken in quick succession are often identical.

What breaks:

  • Ordering rows by created_at (or any time.Now() column), then asserting the exact order. Equal timestamps fall through to the next sort key.
  • if after.After(before) between two operations that run back to back.
  • if elapsed > 0 for a measured duration.

The pattern that bites hardest: ORDER BY created_at, id where id is a random UUID. On Unix the timestamps differ and the test always passes. On Windows they tie, id decides, and the test fails about half the time for two rows.

What to do:

  1. Give ordered records a tie-breaker that follows insertion order, not a random one: a UUIDv7 (uuid.NewV7() from github.com/google/uuid), a database sequence, or an explicit sequence column. UUIDv7 values created by one process keep increasing even within a millisecond, and they sort correctly as uuid in PostgreSQL and as text in SQLite.
  2. If the order within a tie truly does not matter to callers, say so in the doc comment and make the test compare as a set (slices.Sort both sides), so the test checks what the code promises.
  3. Assert d >= 0, not d > 0, for durations. testutil.AssertDurationNonNegative does this.
  4. Never time.Sleep for a few milliseconds to force a different timestamp. It lowers the odds without removing the failure.

docs.title: Path separators and permissions
docs.text:
• Build paths with filepath.Join, and compare with filepath.ToSlash when a test expects a fixed string. fs.NormalizePath and fs.OSPath convert.
  • File mode bits other than read-only are not enforced on Windows. Do not assert 0600 after a write, and skip permission-denied tests with fs.PermissionsEnforced() instead of a runtime.GOOS check, so the condition is named once. fs.CheckPrivate is the owner-only assertion that is correct on both. fs.IsExecutable replaces mode checks.
  • Home and config directories use USERPROFILE and APPDATA, not HOME. testutil and paths set and resolve both.

docs.title: Files that are still open
docs.text:
Windows refuses to delete or rename an open file. Close files and databases before t.TempDir cleanup runs, using t.Cleanup in reverse order of opening, and check the Close error.

This applies to a test that simulates a crash by returning early, for example from a hook between "temporary file created" and "renamed". A real crash closes the process's handles; the simulation must close the handle too, and leave the file, or Windows cannot remove it and the next step and the temporary directory cleanup both fail.

docs.title: File locks and directory flushes
docs.text: Use fs.Lock rather than syscall.Flock, which does not exist on Windows, and fs.SyncDir rather than opening a directory to Sync it, which fails there. Both are tested against a second process in this module.

docs.title: Process and signals
docs.text: There is no SIGTERM, and process groups work differently. Use process.Signal and process.SetDetached rather than syscall directly.

docs.title: Line endings
docs.text: Git may check out text files with CRLF. Compare golden files after normalizing \r\n to \n, or mark them -text in .gitattributes.

docs.title: Catching these before CI
docs.text:
• Run the test suite with -count=20 for any test that orders rows or compares times. Ties show up on Unix too when the operations are fast enough, and repetition exposes order assumptions that happen to pass.
  • Keep a Windows job in CI from the first commit rather than adding it when the project is mature.
  • Review any ORDER BY with a non-deterministic final key.

docs.title: process: signals, liveness, exec
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/process"

docs.title: Stopping a process
docs.text:
Windows has no SIGTERM.

err := process.Signal(pid)         // SIGTERM on Unix, Kill on Windows
err = process.FindAndSignal(pid)   // finds the process first

docs.title: Detached children
docs.text:
cmd := exec.Command("myapp", "serve")
process.SetDetached(cmd) // its own process group on Unix
err := cmd.Start()

docs.title: Is it still the same process?
docs.text:
A file that records a PID goes stale when the process dies, and the system can give the same PID to an unrelated process. Compare the start time.

ok, err := process.Exists(rec.PID)

started, err := process.StartTime(rec.PID)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, process.ErrNotFound):
    // gone
case err == nil && started.Sub(rec.StartedAt).Abs() > 2*time.Second:
    // the PID was reused by a different process
}
Function Behavior Exists(pid) Whether the process is running. A process owned by another user counts as running StartTime(pid) The start time, or ErrNotFound

On Unix the start time comes from ps and has one-second resolution, so allow a tolerance when comparing. On Windows it is the creation time. A PID of zero or less is rejected, because on Unix it addresses a process group.

docs.title: Replacing the current process
docs.text:
err := process.Exec(path, []string{"claude", "--resume", id})

Unix replaces the process. Windows cannot, so it runs the program as a child with the terminal attached and exits with its status. It returns only on failure.

docs.title: testutil: tests that behave the same everywhere
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/testutil"

docs.title: Home directory
docs.text:
func TestConfig(t *testing.T) {
    home := testutil.SetTempHomeDir(t)
    // os.UserHomeDir() now returns home on every platform
}

It sets both HOME and USERPROFILE, because Windows reads the second, and removes the directory when the test ends.

docs.title: Durations
docs.text:
The Windows clock advances in steps of about 15.6 ms, so a fast operation can measure as zero.

testutil.AssertDurationNonNegative(t, elapsed)
if testutil.DurationNonNegative(elapsed) { /* ... */ }

Assert that a duration is not negative, never that it is positive.

docs.title: Capturing output
docs.text:
out, err := testutil.CaptureStdout(func() { fmt.Println("hi") })
stdout, stderr, err := testutil.CaptureOutput(func() { /* ... */ })

The pipe is read concurrently, which avoids the deadlock a large write causes on Windows when a test reads only after the function returns.

See also Writing tests that pass on Windows.

docs.title: tsync: comparing timestamps
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/tsync"

Filesystems keep modification times at different precision: NTFS about 100 ns (sometimes 2 s), ext4 and APFS nanoseconds, FAT32 2 s, network drives anything. Comparing times exactly across them reports files as changed when they are not.

if tsync.Equal(a.ModTime(), b.ModTime()) { /* same, within a second */ }
if tsync.After(a.ModTime(), b.ModTime()) { /* definitely newer */ }

tsync.EqualWithTolerance(t1, t2, tsync.FAT32Tolerance)
newest := tsync.Newer(t1, t2)
stored := tsync.TruncateToSecond(time.Now())
Constant Value For DefaultTolerance 1 s Mixed platforms and network drives FAT32Tolerance 2 s FAT32 HighPrecisionTolerance 100 ms NTFS, ext4, APFS

Compare returns -1, 0 or 1 with the tolerance applied, and the Before, After, Equal and Compare families have a WithTolerance form. Truncate(t, precision) normalizes a time before storing or comparing it.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.1.0
docs.text: This is the initial release of oscompat, a cross-platform OS compatibility library for Go.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: oscompat provides abstractions for OS-specific behaviors that differ between Windows and Unix-like systems (Linux, macOS). Rather than scattering runtime.GOOS checks throughout application code, oscompat encapsulates these differences in reusable, well-tested packages.

docs.title: id - Unique Identifier Generation
docs.text:
Cryptographically secure ID generation using crypto/rand.

Problem solved: Time-based ID generation (e.g., time.Now().UnixNano()) is unreliable on Windows due to the system clock's coarse resolution (~15.6ms vs nanoseconds on Unix), causing ID collisions when generating multiple IDs rapidly.

Key functions:

  • Generate(byteLen int) - Generate custom-length hex ID
  • Generate16() - Generate 16-character hex ID (8 random bytes)
  • Generate32() - Generate 32-character hex ID (16 random bytes)

docs.title: process - Process Management
docs.text:
Cross-platform process signal and detachment handling.

Problem solved: Unix has SIGTERM for graceful termination and Setpgid for process groups; Windows has neither.

Key functions:

  • SetDetached(cmd) - Configure command to run detached from parent
  • Signal(pid) - Send termination signal (SIGTERM on Unix, Kill on Windows)
  • FindAndSignal(pid) - Find process by PID and send termination signal

docs.title: paths - Directory Resolution
docs.text:
Platform-appropriate configuration and data directory resolution.

Problem solved: Applications need standard directories that vary by platform:

Directory Type Linux (XDG) macOS Windows User Config ~/.config ~/Library/Application Support %APPDATA% User Data ~/.local/share ~/Library/Application Support %LOCALAPPDATA% User Cache ~/.cache ~/Library/Caches %LOCALAPPDATA%\cache System Config /etc /etc %ProgramData%

Key functions:

  • Home() - User's home directory
  • AppConfig(name), AppData(name), AppCache(name) - App-specific directories (auto-creates)
  • UserConfig(), UserData(), UserCache(), UserRuntime() - Base user directories
  • SystemConfig(), SystemAppConfig(name) - System-wide directories

docs.title: fs - Filesystem Utilities
docs.text:
Cross-platform path handling, permissions, and validation.

Problems solved:

  • File permissions (0755, 0644) are Unix-centric; Windows ignores them
  • Path separators differ (/ vs )
  • Path traversal attacks must handle both separator types
  • Case sensitivity differs (Windows is case-insensitive)

Key functions:

  • ValidatePath(), ValidatePathStrict() - Detect directory traversal attacks
  • NormalizePath(), OSPath() - Convert between normalized and OS-specific paths
  • SafeJoin() - Path joining with traversal protection
  • MkdirAll(), WriteFile() - Directory/file creation with sensible defaults
  • IsCaseSensitive(), PathEqual(), PathHasPrefix() - Case-aware path comparison
  • Birthtime(), BirthtimeInfo() - File creation time (where supported)

Permission constants: DefaultDirPerm (0755), DefaultFilePerm (0644), PrivateDirPerm (0700), PrivateFilePerm (0600)

docs.title: tsync - Timestamp Utilities
docs.text:
Tolerant timestamp comparison for file synchronization.

Problem solved: Filesystem timestamp precision varies dramatically:

Filesystem Precision Linux ext4/XFS nanosecond Windows NTFS ~100ns (sometimes 2s) FAT32 2 seconds Network drives varies widely

Key functions:

  • Equal(), Before(), After() - Compare with default 1-second tolerance
  • EqualWithTolerance(), BeforeWithTolerance(), AfterWithTolerance() - Custom tolerance
  • Compare(), CompareWithTolerance() - Three-way comparison (-1/0/+1)
  • Truncate(), TruncateToSecond() - Normalize precision for storage
  • FromTimespec(), FromTimeval() - Convert syscall time structures

Tolerance constants: DefaultTolerance (1s), FAT32Tolerance (2s), HighPrecisionTolerance (100ms)

docs.title: localnet - Local IPC
docs.text:
Cross-platform inter-process communication.

Problem solved: Unix domain sockets don't exist on Windows (or have limited support).

Platform Implementation Unix/Linux/macOS Unix domain sockets in /tmp or $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR Windows TCP on localhost with port discovery via file

Key functions:

  • Listen(name) - Create local listener for IPC
  • Dial(name) - Connect to local server
  • SocketPath(name) - Get path/address for documentation
  • Cleanup(name) - Remove stale socket/port files after crash

docs.title: Platform Support
docs.text:
All packages are tested on:

  • Linux (ubuntu-latest)
  • macOS (macos-latest)
  • Windows (windows-latest)

CI runs on Go 1.24.x and 1.25.x.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: New testutil package for cross-platform stdout/stderr capture in tests.

docs.title: New Package: testutil
docs.text: The testutil package provides utilities for capturing stdout and stderr during function execution, useful for testing CLI output.

docs.title: Problem Solved
docs.text: Capturing stdout/stderr for testing requires careful handling of file descriptor manipulation. This is error-prone and varies subtly across platforms.

docs.title: Key Functions
docs.text:
• CaptureStdout(fn) - Execute function and capture its stdout
  • CaptureStderr(fn) - Execute function and capture its stderr
  • CaptureOutput(fn) - Execute function and capture both stdout and stderr

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/testutil"

func TestMyCommand(t *testing.T) {
    stdout := testutil.CaptureStdout(func() {
        myCommand.Execute()
    })

    if !strings.Contains(stdout, "expected output") {
        t.Errorf("unexpected output: %s", stdout)
    }
}

})

After (v0.3.0):

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: Cross-platform executable detection for file permission checks.

docs.title: fs.IsExecutable
docs.text:
Detect whether a file is executable in a cross-platform way.

Problem solved: On Unix, executability is determined by permission bits (0111). On Windows, there are no permission bits; executability is determined by file extension (.exe, .bat, .cmd, etc.).

docs.title: Key Functions
docs.text: Function Description IsExecutable(path) Check if file at path is executable IsExecutableInfo(info) Check executability using existing fs.FileInfo

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/fs"

// Check by path
if fs.IsExecutable("/usr/bin/git") {
    fmt.Println("git is executable")
}

// Check with existing FileInfo (avoids extra stat call)
info, _ := os.Stat(path)
if fs.IsExecutableInfo(info) {
    fmt.Println("file is executable")
}

docs.title: Platform Behavior
docs.text: Platform How Executability is Determined Unix/Linux/macOS File has execute permission (mode & 0111 != 0) Windows File extension is .exe, .bat, .cmd, .com, or .ps1

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: Cross-platform test utilities for home directory and duration assertions.

docs.title: testutil.SetTempHomeDir
docs.text:
Set a temporary directory as the home directory for the duration of a test, handling cross-platform differences automatically.

Problem solved: os.UserHomeDir() reads different environment variables on different platforms:

Platform Environment Variable Unix/Linux/macOS HOME Windows USERPROFILE

Tests that only set HOME will fail on Windows when code uses os.UserHomeDir().

Solution:

import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/testutil"

func TestConfigLoading(t *testing.T) {
    tmpDir := testutil.SetTempHomeDir(t)

    // os.UserHomeDir() now returns tmpDir on all platforms
    config, err := LoadConfig() // Uses home directory internally
    // ...
}

The function:

  • Creates a temporary directory via t.TempDir()
  • Sets both HOME and USERPROFILE environment variables
  • Automatically restores original values when test completes (via t.Setenv)
  • Returns the temporary directory path for test use

docs.title: Duration Assertion Utilities
docs.text:
New utilities for Windows-safe duration assertions in tests.

Problem solved: Windows has a system timer resolution of approximately 15.6ms, which can cause timing-based tests to report slightly negative durations due to clock drift between measurements.

Function Description DurationNonNegative(d) Returns true if duration >= -WindowsTimerResolution AssertDurationNonNegative(t, d, msg) Test helper that fails if duration is too negative WindowsTimerResolution Constant: 16ms tolerance for Windows timer resolution

Example:

import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/testutil"

func TestOperationTiming(t *testing.T) {
    start := time.Now()
    doOperation()
    elapsed := time.Since(start)

    // Windows-safe: allows small negative values due to timer resolution
    testutil.AssertDurationNonNegative(t, elapsed, "operation duration")
}

docs.title: process.Exists and process.StartTime
docs.text:
Problem solved: a file that records a PID, such as a lock file or a session record, goes stale when the process dies. The system can then hand the same PID to an unrelated process, so "does this PID exist?" gives a wrong answer.

Solution: compare the process's start time with the recorded one.

import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/process"

started, err := process.StartTime(rec.PID)
if errors.Is(err, process.ErrNotFound) {
    // the process is gone
}
if err == nil && started.Sub(rec.StartedAt).Abs() > 2*time.Second {
    // the PID was reused by a different process
}
Function Behavior Exists(pid) Reports whether the process is running. A process owned by another user counts as running StartTime(pid) Returns the start time, or ErrNotFound

On Unix the start time comes from ps and has one-second resolution, so allow a small tolerance when comparing. On Windows it is the process creation time, read with GetProcessTimes, using only the standard library. PIDs of zero or less are rejected, because on Unix they address process groups.

docs.title: process.Exec
docs.text:
Problem solved: a launcher that wants to hand the terminal to another program, such as an editor or an agent CLI, wants the program to replace it. Windows cannot replace a running process.

Solution:

err := process.Exec(path, []string{"claude", "--resume", id})
// Unix: replaces this process. Windows: runs a child with the terminal
// attached and exits with its status. Returns only on failure.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: go get github.com/grokify/oscompat@v0.6.0

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: No breaking changes. The module still has no dependencies outside the standard library.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: A cancellable file lock, directory sync and owner-only permission checks in fs, so modules can stop keeping platform-specific files of their own, and a test that enforces that oscompat itself has no dependencies.

docs.title: fs.Lock
docs.text:
Problem solved: mutual exclusion between processes on a file needs syscall.Flock on Unix and LockFileEx on Windows, which means a _unix.go, a _windows.go and a stub for everything else in every module that needs it.

Solution:

import "github.com/grokify/oscompat/fs"

unlock, err := fs.Lock(ctx, "/var/lib/myapp/state.lock")
if err != nil {
    return err // the context's error, or fs.ErrLockUnsupported
}
defer unlock()
Behavior Detail Waiting Polls until the lock is free or the context ends, then returns the context's error Release Calling the returned function releases it, and is safe to call twice; the operating system also releases it if the process exits, however it exits Scope Two calls in one process exclude each other, as two processes do Advisory It excludes only callers that also take it Unsupported platform fs.ErrLockUnsupported, so a caller can fail closed rather than proceed unlocked

The lock file is created with owner-only permissions.

docs.title: fs.SyncDir
docs.text:
Problem solved: after writing a file to a temporary name and renaming it over the target, the rename is only durable once the directory is flushed. Unix lets you open a directory and Sync it; Windows does not.

Solution:

if err := fs.SyncDir(filepath.Dir(path)); err != nil {
    return err
}

On Windows, and on platforms with no way to ask, it does nothing and returns nil, because there a rename is atomic and nothing stronger is available.

docs.title: Permission checks
docs.text:
Problem solved: code that refuses a world-readable key file, and tests that assert 0600, are wrong on Windows, where modes are not enforced.

if fs.PermissionsEnforced() { /* false on Windows */ }

info, _ := os.Stat(path)
if err := fs.CheckPrivate(info); errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotPrivate) {
    // group or others can access it
}

err := fs.ChmodPrivate(f) // 0600 on an open file
Function Behavior PermissionsEnforced() Whether the platform enforces mode bits IsPrivate(info) Owner-only; always true where modes are not enforced CheckPrivate(info) An error matching ErrNotPrivate that names the mode; nil where modes are not enforced ChmodPrivate(f) Restricts an open file to its owner; a failure is ignored where modes are not enforced

docs.title: Policy test
docs.text: The module imports the standard library and itself, and nothing else, so any module can import it. policy_test.go fails on a require, replace or tool directive, a go.sum, or an import from outside the standard library and the module. See the policy.

docs.text:

  • The portable tests guide covers permission assertions with fs.PermissionsEnforced(), closing handles in simulated-crash tests, and the lock and directory sync.
